claim: Blockade of IL-17A failed to modify anti-CD40-induced systemic or intestinal disease in B6Rag1-/- mice.
source: However, blockade of IL-17A failed to modify anti-CD40-induced systemic or intestinal disease (Figure 1A,B), indicating that IL-17A is dispensable for development of acute colitis in this model.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B comparing weight loss and histopathology scores between anti-IL-17A treated and control mice.

claim: IL-17A is dispensable for development of acute colitis in the anti-CD40 model.
source: However, blockade of IL-17A failed to modify anti-CD40-induced systemic or intestinal disease (Figure 1A,B), indicating that IL-17A is dispensable for development of acute colitis in this model.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of IL-17A blockade on disease parameters.

claim: Blocking IL-17F failed to modify anti-CD40-induced disease.
source: Blocking the closely related molecule IL-17F also failed to modify disease (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with neutralising anti-IL-22 mAb had no effect on systemic disease or colitis in the proximal colon.
source: Like IL-17 blockade, treatment with a neutralising anti-IL-22 mAb had no effect on systemic disease or colitis in the proximal colon (Figure 1A&B), indicating that in our facility, IL-22 is also redundant for disease induction in this model.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A&B comparing anti-IL-22 treated mice with controls.

claim: IL-22 is redundant for disease induction in the anti-CD40 colitis model.
source: Like IL-17 blockade, treatment with a neutralising anti-IL-22 mAb had no effect on systemic disease or colitis in the proximal colon (Figure 1A&B), indicating that in our facility, IL-22 is also redundant for disease induction in this model.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of IL-22 blockade on disease parameters.

claim: Blockade of IL-17A and anti-IL-22 reduced intestinal inflammation but not systemic disease.
source: However, blockade of IL-17A and anti-IL-22 reduced intestinal inflammation but not systemic disease indicating redundant roles for IL-17A and IL-22 in the intestinal inflammatory response (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing combined blockade effects.

claim: IL-17A and IL-22 have redundant roles in the intestinal inflammatory response.
source: However, blockade of IL-17A and anti-IL-22 reduced intestinal inflammation but not systemic disease indicating redundant roles for IL-17A and IL-22 in the intestinal inflammatory response (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that combined blockade reduces intestinal inflammation while single blockades do not.

claim: Administration of anti-GM-CSF blocking mAb reduced both weight loss and severity of colitis in anti-CD40 treated mice.
source: Strikingly, administration of an anti-GM-CSF blocking mAb reduced both weight loss (Figure 1C) and severity of colitis (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D comparing anti-GM-CSF treated mice with controls.

claim: Amelioration of colitis with GM-CSF blockade was similar to that observed with anti-IL-23R mAb treatment.
source: Indeed amelioration of colitis with GM-CSF blockade was similar to that observed with anti-IL-23R mAb treatment.
evidence: Supported by comparison of treatment effects shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Similar effects of GM-CSF blockade were observed in bacteria-induced innate colitis following Helicobacter hepaticus infection of 129SvEv Rag2-/- mice.
source: Similar effects of GM-CSF blockade were also observed in bacteria-induced innate colitis following Helicobacter hepaticus infection of 129SvEv Rag2-/- mice (Figure1—figure supplement 2) supporting a pivotal role for this cytokine in both T cell dependent and innate colitis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: GM-CSF plays a pivotal role in both T cell dependent and innate colitis.
source: Similar effects of GM-CSF blockade were also observed in bacteria-induced innate colitis following Helicobacter hepaticus infection of 129SvEv Rag2-/- mice (Figure1—figure supplement 2) supporting a pivotal role for this cytokine in both T cell dependent and innate colitis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GM-CSF blockade is effective in multiple colitis models.

claim: GM-CSF has been shown to promote CNS inflammation through effects on inflammatory monocytes.
source: GM-CSF has been shown to promote CNS inflammation through effects on inflammatory monocytes (Croxford et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Croxford et al., 2015.

claim: GM-CSF blockade led to a marked reduction in the number of inflammatory monocytes in the colon of anti-CD40 treated mice.
source: Consistent with this and in line with a recent report (Song et al., 2015) GM-CSF blockade led to a marked reduction in the number of inflammatory monocytes in the colon of anti-CD40 treated mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and citation to Song et al., 2015.

claim: The number of neutrophils and eosinophils decreased following GM-CSF blockade, but this was not significant.
source: The number of neutrophils and eosinophils also decreased, but this was not significant.
evidence: Supported by experimental data, though statistical significance was not reached.

claim: GM-CSF blockade was accompanied by an increase in both the percentage and total number of CD11b- CD103+ dendritic cells.
source: These changes were accompanied by an increase in both the percentage and total number of CD11b- CD103+ dendritic cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Only a small proportion of epithelial, stromal or lineage positive cells expressed GM-CSF.
source: Only a small proportion of epithelial, stromal or lineage positive (CD11b, CD11c, Gr-1, B220, CD49b) cells expressed GM-CSF (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The majority of lineage positive GM-CSF producers were NK cells.
source: The majority of these lineage positive GM-CSF producers were NK cells, and they expressed a lower amount of GM-CSF than ILCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A & B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A & B.

claim: NK cells expressed a lower amount of GM-CSF than ILCs.
source: The majority of these lineage positive GM-CSF producers were NK cells, and they expressed a lower amount of GM-CSF than ILCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A & B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A & B.

claim: NK cells were not required for the development of anti-CD40 mediated colitis.
source: However, using Rag and IL-15 receptor double deficient mice that lack NK cells (Lodolce et al., 1998), we found, as previously reported (Vonarbourg et al., 2010), that NK cells were not required for the development of anti-CD40 mediated colitis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in NK cell-deficient mice shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–F and citations to Lodolce et al., 1998 and Vonarbourg et al., 2010.

claim: A significant proportion of ILCs were capable of producing GM-CSF, even in the healthy intestine.
source: By contrast, a significant proportion of ILCs were capable of producing GM-CSF, even in the healthy intestine, and this proportion increased during colitis (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The proportion of ILCs producing GM-CSF increased during colitis.
source: By contrast, a significant proportion of ILCs were capable of producing GM-CSF, even in the healthy intestine, and this proportion increased during colitis (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B comparing steady state and colitis conditions.

claim: GM-CSF+ ILCs were CCR6-, cKit- and NKR-, and expressed only low amounts of T-bet.
source: Consistent with an IL-23-dependent ILC3 phenotype, GM-CSF+ ILCs were CCR6-, cKit- and NKR-, and expressed only low amounts of T-bet (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: IL-12 had no effect on either the proportion of GM-CSF-expressing ILCs or the amount of GM-CSF per cell.
source: IL-12 had no effect on either the proportion of GM-CSF-expressing ILCs or the amount of GM-CSF per cell (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Culture with IL-23 increased both the proportion of GM-CSF expressing ILCs as well as GM-CSF production per cell.
source: By contrast and contrary to a previous study using sorted ILC3s (Mortha et al., 2014), culture with IL-23 increased both the proportion of GM-CSF expressing ILCs as well as GM-CSF production per cell (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 2C and contrasted with citation to Mortha et al., 2014.

claim: Il23a mRNA expression peaked at day 1 following anti-CD40 treatment and rapidly declined.
source: Analysis of Il23a mRNA expression within colonic tissue revealed a peak in expression at day 1 following anti-CD40 treatment that rapidly declined but was followed by increased expression of Csf2, the gene for GM-CSF, at day 3 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Csf2 mRNA expression increased at day 3 following anti-CD40 treatment.
source: Analysis of Il23a mRNA expression within colonic tissue revealed a peak in expression at day 1 following anti-CD40 treatment that rapidly declined but was followed by increased expression of Csf2, the gene for GM-CSF, at day 3 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The increase in both Il23a and Csf2 was abrogated in mice treated with a blocking antibody to GM-CSF.
source: The increase in both Il23a and Csf2 was abrogated in mice treated with a blocking antibody to GM-CSF, indicating that GM-CSF may be required to maintain and amplify expression of Il23a.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data comparing anti-GM-CSF treated and control mice shown in Figure 2D.

claim: GM-CSF may be required to maintain and amplify expression of Il23a.
source: The increase in both Il23a and Csf2 was abrogated in mice treated with a blocking antibody to GM-CSF, indicating that GM-CSF may be required to maintain and amplify expression of Il23a.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GM-CSF blockade prevents Il23a upregulation.

claim: PMA and ionomycin stimulated blood ILC3s produced GM-CSF with very little production from other ILC subsets.
source: PMA and ionomycin stimulated blood ILC3s produced GM-CSF with very little production from other ILC subsets (Figure 3A&B, gating strategy in Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from human blood samples shown in Figure 3A&B.

claim: A greater proportion of ILCs produced GM-CSF than did T cells from the same healthy donors.
source: Indeed, a greater proportion of ILCs produced GM-CSF than did T cells from the same healthy donors (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data comparing ILCs and T cells shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ILCs secreting GM-CSF are further enriched in the colon compared to blood.
source: ILCs secreting GM-CSF are further enriched in the colon (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data comparing blood and colon ILCs shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The proportion of blood ILCs capable of GM-CSF production along with other disease-associated cytokines such as IFNγ and TNFα was greater in IBD patients than in healthy controls.
source: Critically, the proportion of blood ILCs capable of GM-CSF production along with other disease-associated cytokines such as IFNγ and TNFα was greater in IBD patients than in healthy controls (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data comparing IBD patients and healthy controls shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There was a significant increase in CSF2 gene expression in the colons of patients with either Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis compared with controls.
source: Analysis of a publically available dataset of colon tissue from healthy controls and IBD patients showed a significant increase in CSF2 gene expression in the colons of patients with either Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis compared with controls (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data from the Leuven cohort shown in Figure 3F.

claim: CSF2 expression was higher in uninflamed biopsies from IBD patients compared with controls.
source: CSF2 expression was also higher in uninflamed biopsies from IBD patients compared with controls.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data from the Oxford cohort shown in Figure 3G.

claim: There was significantly greater CSF2 expression in lesional areas in active disease compared to uninflamed areas.
source: There was significantly greater expression again in lesional areas in active disease, suggesting that GM-CSF expression correlates with, and may be a driver of, inflammation in IBD.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data from the Oxford cohort shown in Figure 3G.

claim: GM-CSF expression correlates with inflammation in IBD.
source: There was significantly greater expression again in lesional areas in active disease, suggesting that GM-CSF expression correlates with, and may be a driver of, inflammation in IBD.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CSF2 expression increases with disease activity.

claim: GM-CSF may be a driver of inflammation in IBD.
source: There was significantly greater expression again in lesional areas in active disease, suggesting that GM-CSF expression correlates with, and may be a driver of, inflammation in IBD.
evidence: Speculative statement based on correlation between CSF2 expression and disease activity.

claim: Under homeostatic conditions ILCs primarily reside within lymphoid aggregate cryptopatch (CP) structures.
source: Under homeostatic conditions ILCs primarily reside within lymphoid aggregate cryptopatch (CP) structures (Figure 4A) and are found only rarely within the non-inflamed lamina propria.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ILCs are found only rarely within the non-inflamed lamina propria.
source: Under homeostatic conditions ILCs primarily reside within lymphoid aggregate cryptopatch (CP) structures (Figure 4A) and are found only rarely within the non-inflamed lamina propria.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Within CP, RORγt+ and IL-7Rα+ ILC3s are present at high density surrounded by CD11c and MHCII expressing cells.
source: Within CP, RORγt+ and IL-7Rα+ ILC3s are present at high density surrounded by CD11c and MHCII expressing cells.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Some ILCs within CP also express CD4, suggesting that some but not all are classical LTi cells.
source: Some of these ILCs within CP also express CD4, suggesting that some but not all are classical LTi cells that are known to be involved in lymphoid organogenesis (Figure 4A).
evidence: Inferred from CD4 expression pattern shown in Figure 4A and established knowledge about LTi cells.

claim: Classical LTi cells are known to be involved in lymphoid organogenesis.
source: Some of these ILCs within CP also express CD4, suggesting that some but not all are classical LTi cells that are known to be involved in lymphoid organogenesis (Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about LTi cell function.

claim: ILCs are known to express IL-23R.
source: In addition to RORγt expression, ILCs are known to express IL-23R (Buonocore et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buonocore et al., 2010.

claim: Il23rgfp/+ Rag-/- mice can be used to study ILC behaviour in vivo.
source: FACS analysis of Rag-deficient mice that express GFP under control of the Il23r demonstrates that these mice can be used to study ILC behaviour in vivo (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B validating the reporter mouse model.

claim: Greater than 90% of ILCs are present within cryptopatches under steady-state conditions.
source: Quantification of ILC localization in 3D indicates that greater than 90% of ILCs are present within cryptopatches under steady-state conditions (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by quantification of imaging data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: IL-23R+ ILCs are positioned in close proximity to a high density of CD11c+ DCs that can be activated by colitogenic stimuli.
source: This suggests that IL-23R+ ILCs are perfectly positioned in close proximity to a high density of CD11c+ DCs that can be activated by colitogenic stimuli.
evidence: Inferred from the spatial organization observed in imaging data.

claim: Il23r mRNA increased in the colon 6 hr following anti-CD40 injection.
source: Indeed Il23r mRNA increased in the colon 6 hr following anti-CD40 injection indicating that the first ILC changes occur in the hours following CD40 stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The first ILC changes occur in the hours following CD40 stimulation.
source: Indeed Il23r mRNA increased in the colon 6 hr following anti-CD40 injection indicating that the first ILC changes occur in the hours following CD40 stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Inferred from the rapid increase in Il23r mRNA expression.

claim: There was a decrease in IL-23R+ ILCs at day 3 following anti-CD40 stimulation.
source: We further examined the changes in IL-23R expression following anti-CD40 stimulation, and found a decrease in IL-23R+ ILCs at day 3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B&C), which may indicate a change in ILC phenotype.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B&C.

claim: The decrease in IL-23R+ ILCs may indicate a change in ILC phenotype.
source: We further examined the changes in IL-23R expression following anti-CD40 stimulation, and found a decrease in IL-23R+ ILCs at day 3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B&C), which may indicate a change in ILC phenotype.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed decrease in IL-23R expression.

claim: There was a transient decrease in the proportion of ILCs expressing RORγt 3 days following anti-CD40 stimulation.
source: In support of this hypothesis, analysis of RORγt protein revealed a transient decrease in the proportion of ILCs expressing it 3 days following anti-CD40 stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D&E), similar to a previous report (Vonarbourg et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D&E and citation to Vonarbourg et al., 2010.

claim: ILCs were much more motile than expected in the steady-state.
source: In the steady-state, ILCs were much more motile than expected.
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy observations shown in Figure 5 and Videos 2-3.

claim: ILCs can be observed to enter and exit the cryptopatch cluster near the basal collagen layer.
source: While little motility could be observed within the cryptopatch, ILCs can be observed to enter and exit the cluster near the basal collagen layer (Figure 5A and Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy data shown in Figure 5A and Videos 2 and 3.

claim: The cryptopatch did not have an obvious point of entry or exit.
source: Interestingly, the cryptopatch did not have an obvious point of entry or exit, implying that trafficking into and out of the structure may be governed by mechanisms different to that of the lymph node.
evidence: Observed from intravital microscopy imaging.

claim: Trafficking into and out of the cryptopatch may be governed by mechanisms different to that of the lymph node.
source: Interestingly, the cryptopatch did not have an obvious point of entry or exit, implying that trafficking into and out of the structure may be governed by mechanisms different to that of the lymph node.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of obvious entry/exit points in cryptopatches.

claim: The average velocity of motile ILCs is approximately 9 μm/min.
source: By gating on motile cells outside the cluster, we could see that the average velocity of motile ILCs (approximately 9 μm/min) is grossly similar to that of other lymphocytes and while cell velocity decreases after treatment with anti-CD40 (Figure 5B), this difference does not appear to affect overall cell trafficking.
evidence: Supported by quantification of intravital microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cell velocity decreases after treatment with anti-CD40.
source: By gating on motile cells outside the cluster, we could see that the average velocity of motile ILCs (approximately 9 μm/min) is grossly similar to that of other lymphocytes and while cell velocity decreases after treatment with anti-CD40 (Figure 5B), this difference does not appear to affect overall cell trafficking.
evidence: Supported by quantification of intravital microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The decrease in cell velocity after anti-CD40 treatment does not appear to affect overall cell trafficking.
source: By gating on motile cells outside the cluster, we could see that the average velocity of motile ILCs (approximately 9 μm/min) is grossly similar to that of other lymphocytes and while cell velocity decreases after treatment with anti-CD40 (Figure 5B), this difference does not appear to affect overall cell trafficking.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that despite velocity changes, trafficking patterns still change.

claim: Just 4–6 hr after anti-CD40 treatment, a greater proportion of ILCs exit the cryptopatch and a smaller proportion enter.
source: In steady-state, roughly equal numbers of cells move toward and away from the cluster; however, just 4–6 hr after anti-CD40 treatment, a greater proportion of cells exit the tissue and a smaller proportion enter (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by quantification of ILC displacement vectors shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The ratio of entering to exiting cells indicates a significant skewing toward egress from cryptopatches after anti-CD40 treatment.
source: The ratio of entering to exiting cells indicates a significant skewing toward egress from cryptopatches (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The shift toward exit that is normally observed after anti-CD40 treatment was strikingly reversed when mice were treated with a GM-CSF blocking antibody 24 hr before imaging.
source: To assess whether GM-CSF may be playing a role in ILC mobilization, we treated mice with anti-GM-CSF 24 hr before imaging. The shift toward exit that is normally observed after anti-CD40 treatment was strikingly reversed when mice were treated with a GM-CSF blocking antibody 24 hr before imaging (Figure 5D and E, Video 6).
evidence: Supported by quantification of ILC trafficking in anti-GM-CSF treated mice shown in Figure 5D and E, Video 6.

claim: ILCs appeared to be adjacent to blood vessels, not within them.
source: It is possible that many of these cells move through blood vessels, but by labelling the blood vessels with texas-red dextran, ILCs appeared to be adjacent to blood vessels, not within them (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy with blood vessel labeling shown in Figure 5F.

claim: ILCs may be mobilizing into the adjacent tissue from cryptopatches.
source: This indicates that ILCs may be mobilizing into the adjacent tissue from cryptopatches.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ILCs are adjacent to but not within blood vessels.

claim: 24 hr after anti-CD40 treatment the chemokines Ccl19 and Ccl2 were increased in the tissue.
source: To understand what impact the early mobilization of ILCs has on the tissue, we looked at several chemokines that could be influencing the development of inflammatory foci. 24 hr after anti-CD40 treatment the chemokines Ccl19 and Ccl2 were increased in the tissue.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The receptor for Ccl19, Ccr7, was increased 24 hr after anti-CD40 treatment.
source: The receptor for Ccl19, Ccr7, was also increased (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Blocking GM-CSF prevented the increase of Ccr7 and Ccl2.
source: Blocking GM-CSF prevented the increase of Ccr7 and Ccl2, supporting the idea that there is cross-talk between the GM-CSF and migration axes.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data comparing anti-GM-CSF treated and control mice shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is cross-talk between the GM-CSF and migration axes.
source: Blocking GM-CSF prevented the increase of Ccr7 and Ccl2, supporting the idea that there is cross-talk between the GM-CSF and migration axes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GM-CSF blockade prevents chemokine upregulation.

claim: It is the lineage positive cells that are capable of responding to the increased tissue chemokines.
source: Staining for CCR7 and CCR2 on lineage+ and ILC subsets suggested that it is the lineage positive cells that are capable of responding to the increased tissue chemokines (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Immune foci are present at the tips of villi in the proximal colon 7 days after anti-CD40 treatment.
source: Histological analysis of the proximal colon 7 days after anti-CD40 treatment showed immune foci at the tips of villi (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining showed colocalization of ILCs with the CD11c positive immune infiltrate.
source: Immunofluorescence staining for CD11c and RORγt showed colocalization of ILCs with the CD11c positive immune infiltrate.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The CD11c positive immune infiltrate may reflect the inflammatory monocytes identified by flow cytometry from colon digests.
source: The latter may reflect the inflammatory monocytes identified by flow cytometry from colon digests (Figure 6D and 1E).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of immunofluorescence and flow cytometry data.

claim: Cryptopatch cellularity decreased after 24 hr following anti-CD40 treatment.
source: Quantification of cryptopatch cellularity from H&E after anti-CD40 treatment showed a decrease in cellularity after 24 hr (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by quantification of histological sections shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The net egress of cells from cryptopatches over a short imaging window corresponds to the loss of cells from the tissue over 24 hr.
source: The net egress of cells from cryptopatches over a short imaging window (Figure 5D) corresponds to the loss of cells from the tissue over 24 hr.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between imaging data and histological quantification.

claim: The decrease in cryptopatch cellularity is followed by an increase in inflammatory infiltrates starting one day later.
source: This decrease is followed by an increase in inflammatory infiltrates starting one day later (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by quantification of cryptopatches and inflammatory infiltrates over time shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Blocking GM-CSF resulted in maintenance of cryptopatch structure.
source: Blocking GM-CSF resulted in maintenance of cryptopatch structure as would be predicted from the imaging data (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence imaging of anti-GM-CSF treated mice shown in Figure 6G.

claim: ILC mobilization from cryptopatches is associated with a decrease in cryptopatch cellularity, increase in tissue chemokines, recruitment of inflammatory cells, and development of inflammatory foci associated with active disease.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that ILC mobilization from cryptopatches is associated with a decrease in cryptopatch cellularity, increase in tissue chemokines, recruitment of inflammatory cells, and development of inflammatory foci associated with active disease.
evidence: Synthesized conclusion from multiple experimental observations.

claim: The results reveal a new IL-23-driven GM-CSF axis that promotes ILC3-mediated acute colitis.
source: The results of this study reveal a new IL-23-driven GM-CSF axis that promotes ILC3-mediated acute colitis.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on all experimental findings.

claim: Innate colitis involves cellular activation, GM-CSF dependent mobilization of IL-23R+ ILCs from cryptopatches, and subsequent perpetuation of the response through separate ILC-containing inflammatory foci and GM-CSF dependent accumulation of inflammatory monocytes.
source: Our data indicate a spatiotemporal model for innate colitis that involves cellular activation, GM-CSF dependent mobilization of IL-23R+ ILCs from cryptopatches, and subsequent perpetuation of the response through separate ILC-containing inflammatory foci and GM-CSF dependent accumulation of inflammatory monocytes.
evidence: Synthesized model based on all experimental observations.

claim: Anti-CD40 induced colitis was IL-17A and IL-17F independent.
source: Although IL-23 dependent, we found that anti-CD40 induced colitis was IL-17A and IL-17F independent in keeping with earlier reports (Figure 1 and Eken et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1 and citation to Eken et al., 2014.

claim: Two recent reports indicated a functional role for IL-22, possibly through neutrophil recruitment.
source: Two recent reports indicated a functional role for IL-22, possibly through neutrophil recruitment (Eken et al., 2014; Song et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eken et al., 2014 and Song et al., 2015.

claim: IL-22 blockade or neutrophil depletion had no impact on the incidence or severity of disease in the anti-CD40 model.
source: However our data show no impact of IL-22 blockade or neutrophil depletion (data not shown) on the incidence or severity of disease in this model.
evidence: Supported by experimental data (neutrophil depletion data not shown).

claim: IL-17A and IL-22 may play a redundant role in driving intestinal inflammation possibly through shared effects on intestinal epithelial cells.
source: By contrast, double blockade of IL-17A and IL-22 reduced colitis severity, indicating that these cytokines may play a redundant role in driving intestinal inflammation possibly through shared effects on intestinal epithelial cells (Liang et al., 2006).
evidence: Inferred from double blockade effects and supported by citation to Liang et al., 2006.

claim: The pathogenic role of IL-22 in CD40-triggered colitis may depend on the presence of microbial factors that also influence IL-17A production in the intestine.
source: The pathogenic role of IL-22 in CD40-triggered colitis may depend on the presence of microbial factors that also influence IL-17A production in the intestine.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of differences between studies.

claim: IL-22 alone was required for the maintenance of bacteria driven innate colitis-associated cancer.
source: Consistent with this, IL-22 alone was required for the maintenance of bacteria driven innate colitis-associated cancer (Kirchberger et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kirchberger et al., 2013.

claim: Context-dependent effector functions mediate the colitogenic potential of IL-23.
source: Together these results suggest that context-dependent effector functions mediate the colitogenic potential of IL-23.
evidence: Inferred from the variable roles of IL-22 and IL-17A in different contexts.

claim: Recent studies have focussed on the role of GM-CSF as an important mediator of IL-23 driven tissue inflammation.
source: Recent studies have focussed on the role of GM-CSF as an important mediator of IL-23 driven tissue inflammation (Codarri et al., 2011; El-Behi et al., 2011; Griseri et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Codarri et al., 2011; El-Behi et al., 2011; Griseri et al., 2012.

claim: GM-CSF played a non-redundant role in both systemic and intestinal inflammation in the anti-CD40 model.
source: We found that GM-CSF played a non-redundant role in both systemic and intestinal inflammation in the anti-CD40 model and was required for bacteria-induced innate colitis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The role of GM-CSF in anti-CD40 mediated systemic disease has been recently reported.
source: The role of GM-CSF in anti-CD40 mediated systemic disease has been recently reported (Song et al., 2015) but effects on colitis were not assessed.
evidence: Supported by citation to Song et al., 2015.

claim: IL-23-responsive ILCs can act as the main source of GM-CSF in an innate model.
source: Our results indicate that IL-23-responsive ILCs can act as the main source of GM-CSF in an innate model.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data showing GM-CSF production by ILCs in Figure 2.

claim: ILCs are potent sources of GM-CSF in humans.
source: Importantly we also find that ILCs are potent sources of GM-CSF in humans, consistent with a previous report describing cytokine-driven GM-CSF production from an NKp44- ILC population (Glatzer et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from human samples in Figure 3 and citation to Glatzer et al., 2013.

claim: GM-CSF is produced by ILC3s in the blood and colon of patients.
source: Our study goes further to show that GM-CSF is produced by ILC3s in the blood and colon of patients.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data from human samples in Figure 3.

claim: The percent of GM-CSF+ ILCs is larger than the percent of GM-CSF+ T cells.
source: The percent of GM-CSF+ ILCs is larger than the percent of GM-CSF+ T cells.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data comparing ILCs and T cells in Figure 3C.

claim: The GM-CSF+ ILC3 population is increased in the blood and colonic tissue of patients with IBD.
source: This GM-CSF+ ILC3 population is increased in the blood and colonic tissue of patients with IBD, indicating commonalities between mouse models and human disease pathogenesis.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and gene expression data from IBD patients in Figure 3.

claim: There are commonalities between mouse models and human disease pathogenesis.
source: This GM-CSF+ ILC3 population is increased in the blood and colonic tissue of patients with IBD, indicating commonalities between mouse models and human disease pathogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from similar findings in mouse and human studies.

claim: IL-23 and GM-CSF may act in an autocrine loop early in the inflammatory response.
source: IL-23 and GM-CSF may act in an autocrine loop early in the early inflammatory response as we found that anti-CD40-induced early colonic IL-23 expression was GM-CSF dependent and that in turn, IL-23 was required for sustained GM-CSF production by ILCs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GM-CSF blockade prevents IL-23 upregulation and IL-23 drives GM-CSF production.

claim: Anti-CD40-induced early colonic IL-23 expression was GM-CSF dependent.
source: IL-23 and GM-CSF may act in an autocrine loop early in the early inflammatory response as we found that anti-CD40-induced early colonic IL-23 expression was GM-CSF dependent and that in turn, IL-23 was required for sustained GM-CSF production by ILCs.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data showing GM-CSF blockade prevents IL-23 upregulation in Figure 2D.

claim: IL-23 was required for sustained GM-CSF production by ILCs.
source: IL-23 and GM-CSF may act in an autocrine loop early in the early inflammatory response as we found that anti-CD40-induced early colonic IL-23 expression was GM-CSF dependent and that in turn, IL-23 was required for sustained GM-CSF production by ILCs.
evidence: Supported by in vitro culture data showing IL-23 drives GM-CSF production in Figure 2C.

claim: A similar positive feedback loop has been described for T cell derived GM-CSF in CNS inflammation.
source: A similar positive feedback loop has been described for T cell derived GM-CSF in CNS inflammation (El-Behi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to El-Behi et al., 2011.

claim: Such a feedback loop would promote more GM-CSF production from ILCs as IL-23 production increases in disease.
source: Such a feedback loop would promote more GM-CSF production from ILCs as IL-23 production increases in disease.
evidence: Inferred from the proposed autocrine loop mechanism.

claim: The role of GM-CSF may be to recruit myeloid cells to sites of inflammation, and impact their ability to coordinate inflammatory responses.
source: The role of GM-CSF may be to recruit myeloid cells to sites of inflammation, and impact their ability to coordinate inflammatory responses, as has recently been shown in EAE (Croxford et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative statement supported by citation to Croxford et al., 2015.

claim: Blocking GM-CSF prevented the accumulation of Ly6C+ inflammatory monocytes following anti-CD40 stimulation.
source: Indeed, we found blocking GM-CSF prevented the accumulation of Ly6C+ inflammatory monocytes following anti-CD40 stimulation, in line with recent evidence for a key role for these cells in driving pathogenesis during anti-CD40 induced colitis (Song et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1E and citation to Song et al., 2015.

claim: There is recent evidence for a key role for inflammatory monocytes in driving pathogenesis during anti-CD40 induced colitis.
source: Indeed, we found blocking GM-CSF prevented the accumulation of Ly6C+ inflammatory monocytes following anti-CD40 stimulation, in line with recent evidence for a key role for these cells in driving pathogenesis during anti-CD40 induced colitis (Song et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Song et al., 2015.

claim: GM-CSF expression also has wider consequences since it affects the behaviour of ILCs within the cryptopatch.
source: However, GM-CSF expression also has wider consequences since it affects the behaviour of ILCs within the cryptopatch.
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy data showing GM-CSF-dependent ILC mobilization in Figure 5.

claim: Functional analyses of ILC populations have mainly been restricted to cytokine production.
source: Functional analyses of ILC populations have mainly been restricted to cytokine production, and recent evidence that they do not recirculate suggested a primarily sedentary role for these cells (Gasteiger et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on review of literature and citation to Gasteiger et al., 2015.

claim: Recent evidence suggests that ILCs do not recirculate.
source: Functional analyses of ILC populations have mainly been restricted to cytokine production, and recent evidence that they do not recirculate suggested a primarily sedentary role for these cells (Gasteiger et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gasteiger et al., 2015.

claim: Cryptopatches may provide a platform for the rapid amplification of the immune response.
source: Cryptopatches may provide a platform for the rapid amplification of the immune response and may provide a potential mechanism by which a very small number of ILCs could initiate an immune cascade that culminates in colonic inflammation.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the spatial organization and dynamics observed.

claim: Cryptopatches may provide a potential mechanism by which a very small number of ILCs could initiate an immune cascade that culminates in colonic inflammation.
source: Cryptopatches may provide a platform for the rapid amplification of the immune response and may provide a potential mechanism by which a very small number of ILCs could initiate an immune cascade that culminates in colonic inflammation.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on all experimental observations.

claim: The anti-CD40 model provided temporal synchronization, which is a feature unique to this model of colitis.
source: The anti-CD40 model provided temporal synchronization, which is a feature unique to this model of colitis.
evidence: Based on established characteristics of the anti-CD40 model.

claim: A subset of ILCs associated with the cryptopatch was migratory under steady-state conditions.
source: To our surprise, a subset of ILCs associated with the cryptopatch was migratory under steady-state conditions.
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy observations shown in Figure 5 and Videos 2-3.

claim: After anti-CD40 treatment, ILC motility shifted toward egress from the cryptopatch.
source: After anti-CD40 treatment, ILC motility shifted toward egress from the cryptopatch.
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy quantification shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: ILCs do not recirculate through the blood.
source: In agreement with data that suggests they do not recirculate through the blood (Gasteiger et al., 2015), ILCs were not observed migrating into the peripheral blood but appeared to crawl directly through the tissue, possibly following a local chemokine gradient.
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy observations and citation to Gasteiger et al., 2015.

claim: ILCs appeared to crawl directly through the tissue, possibly following a local chemokine gradient.
source: In agreement with data that suggests they do not recirculate through the blood (Gasteiger et al., 2015), ILCs were not observed migrating into the peripheral blood but appeared to crawl directly through the tissue, possibly following a local chemokine gradient.
evidence: Inferred from intravital microscopy observations showing ILCs adjacent to but not within blood vessels.

claim: There was an early peak in mRNA expression of the chemokines Ccl2, Ccl19 and its receptor Ccr7 in the tissue.
source: Consistent with chemokine-induced migration of ILCs, we found an early peak in mRNA expression of the chemokines Ccl2, Ccl19 and its receptor Ccr7 in the tissue, suggesting an early role for CCR7 and CCR2.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The data suggest an early role for CCR7 and CCR2.
source: Consistent with chemokine-induced migration of ILCs, we found an early peak in mRNA expression of the chemokines Ccl2, Ccl19 and its receptor Ccr7 in the tissue, suggesting an early role for CCR7 and CCR2.
evidence: Inferred from the early upregulation of these chemokines and receptors.

claim: CCR7 or CCR2 expression on ILCs was not detected in anti-CD40 induced colitis.
source: Despite data showing that migration of LTi ILC3s from the gut to the mesenteric lymph nodes is dependent on CCR7 expression (Mackley et al., 2015), expression of CCR7 on ILCs was not assessed in that study and we were unable to identify CCR7 or CCR2 on intestinal ILC3s in anti-CD40 induced colitis.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Migration of LTi ILC3s from the gut to the mesenteric lymph nodes is dependent on CCR7 expression.
source: Despite data showing that migration of LTi ILC3s from the gut to the mesenteric lymph nodes is dependent on CCR7 expression (Mackley et al., 2015), expression of CCR7 on ILCs was not assessed in that study and we were unable to identify CCR7 or CCR2 on intestinal ILC3s in anti-CD40 induced colitis.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mackley et al., 2015.

claim: The lack of CCR7 on ILCs argues against CCR7 driven chemotaxis of the ILCs.
source: While this argues against CCR7 driven chemotaxis of the ILCs, it does not preclude an organizational function for ILCs in the tissue driven by other mediators.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of CCR7 expression on ILCs.

claim: The data indicate a role for GM-CSF in the net egress of ILCs from cryptopatches in anti-CD40 induced colitis.
source: Indeed, our data indicate a role for GM-CSF in the net egress of ILCs from cryptopatches in anti-CD40 induced colitis.
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy data showing GM-CSF blockade prevents ILC egress in Figure 5.

claim: Increased amounts of ccl2 and ccr7 mRNA in the colon were GM-CSF-dependent.
source: Similarly, increased amounts of ccl2 and ccr7 mRNA in the colon were also GM-CSF-dependent, as was accumulation of inflammatory monocytes which also express CCR7 and CCR2 (Tsou et al., 2007; Förster et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A and citations to Tsou et al., 2007 and Förster et al., 2008.

claim: Accumulation of inflammatory monocytes was GM-CSF-dependent.
source: Similarly, increased amounts of ccl2 and ccr7 mRNA in the colon were also GM-CSF-dependent, as was accumulation of inflammatory monocytes which also express CCR7 and CCR2 (Tsou et al., 2007; Förster et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1E and citations.

claim: Inflammatory monocytes express CCR7 and CCR2.
source: Similarly, increased amounts of ccl2 and ccr7 mRNA in the colon were also GM-CSF-dependent, as was accumulation of inflammatory monocytes which also express CCR7 and CCR2 (Tsou et al., 2007; Förster et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tsou et al., 2007 and Förster et al., 2008.

claim: The data are compatible with a model in which GM-CSF-dependent activation of ILCs leads to exit from the cryptopatch to the villus tip, coinciding with recruitment of CCR7 and CCR2 expressing inflammatory monocytes through a CCL19 and CCL2 gradient, culminating in tissue damage.
source: Together, the data are compatible with a model in which GM-CSF-dependent activation of ILCs leads to exit from the cryptopatch to the villus tip. This coincides with the recruitment of CCR7 and CCR2 expressing inflammatory monocytes through a CCL19 and CCL2 gradient, culminating in tissue damage.
evidence: Synthesized model based on all experimental observations.

claim: Sustained production of GM-CSF by ILCs in inflammatory foci could recruit inflammatory progenitor cells and contribute to differentiation of myeloid effector cells.
source: Sustained production of GM-CSF by ILCs in inflammatory foci could recruit inflammatory progenitor cells and contribute to differentiation of myeloid effector cells.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the role of GM-CSF in inflammatory foci.

claim: GM-CSF has been shown to control the differentiation of inflammatory monocytes.
source: GM-CSF has been shown to control the differentiation of inflammatory monocytes (Lenzo et al., 2012), and this population was markedly reduced following anti-GM-CSF treatment.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lenzo et al., 2012 and experimental data in Figure 1E.

claim: GM-CSF may impact on myeloid cell pathways through altered haematopoiesis and accumulation of granulocyte macrophage progenitors as described in T cell dependent colitis.
source: GM-CSF may also impact on this pathway through altered haematopoiesis and accumulation of granulocyte macrophage progenitors as described in T cell dependent colitis (Griseri et al., 2012).
evidence: Speculative statement supported by citation to Griseri et al., 2012.

claim: IL-23 has been suggested as a therapeutic target in IBD.
source: IL-23 has been suggested as a therapeutic target in IBD (Bowman et al., 2006; Uhlig et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bowman et al., 2006 and Uhlig et al., 2006.

claim: Neutralisation of GM-CSF is as efficacious as blockade of IL-23 in mouse models.
source: However, our studies indicate that neutralisation of GM-CSF is as efficacious as blockade of IL-23 in mouse models.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing anti-GM-CSF and anti-IL-23R treatments in Figure 1.

claim: Increases in GM-CSF secreting ILCs are a feature of IBD.
source: In addition, increases in GM-CSF secreting ILCs are a feature of IBD.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry and gene expression data from IBD patients in Figure 3.

claim: There are clear host protective functions of GM-CSF in the intestine.
source: However, targeting GM-CSF may not be straightforward in IBD as there are clear host protective functions of GM-CSF in the intestine (Sainathan et al., 2008; Bernasconi et al., 2010; Hirata et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sainathan et al., 2008; Bernasconi et al., 2010; Hirata et al., 2010.

claim: Neutralising anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies are increased in IBD, particularly in patients with ileal and stricturing disease.
source: Indeed neutralising anti-GM-CSF autoantibodies are increased in IBD, particularly in patients with ileal and stricturing disease (Han et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Han et al., 2009.

claim: Administration of recombinant GM-CSF (sargramostim) has been used to treat Crohn's disease.
source: Furthermore, administration of recombinant GM-CSF (sargramostim) has been used to treat Crohn's disease (Korzenik et al., 2005) although further trials did not show any substantial benefit of GM-CSF treatment (Roth et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Korzenik et al., 2005 and Roth et al., 2012.

claim: Further trials did not show any substantial benefit of GM-CSF treatment for Crohn's disease.
source: Furthermore, administration of recombinant GM-CSF (sargramostim) has been used to treat Crohn's disease (Korzenik et al., 2005) although further trials did not show any substantial benefit of GM-CSF treatment (Roth et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roth et al., 2012.

claim: Anti-GM-CSF is being tested in clinical trials for the treatment of multiple sclerosis.
source: Despite these issues, in light of recent developments testing anti-GM-CSF in clinical trials for the treatment of other inflammatory conditions such as multiple sclerosis (Constantinescu et al., 2015) it will be interesting to see if subgroups of patients with hyperinflammatory innate immune activation-driven IBD could benefit from GM-CSF blockade.
evidence: Supported by citation to Constantinescu et al., 2015.

claim: Subgroups of patients with hyperinflammatory innate immune activation-driven IBD could benefit from GM-CSF blockade.
source: Despite these issues, in light of recent developments testing anti-GM-CSF in clinical trials for the treatment of other inflammatory conditions such as multiple sclerosis (Constantinescu et al., 2015) it will be interesting to see if subgroups of patients with hyperinflammatory innate immune activation-driven IBD could benefit from GM-CSF blockade.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential therapeutic application.
